narrative:
The model determined that you have a 90% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for predicted success, this led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year ranking also contributed noticeably in the same direction, though less strongly. Your undergraduate GPA added a smaller but still meaningful push toward a negative outcome.

All three of these academic indicators placed you well below the typical student who is accepted. While many admitted students rank around the middle of their class, you ranked near the bottom in both your first and third years. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 also sits substantially below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants. These consistent signals of academic performance outweighed other details such as your middle-income background, LSAT score of 30, and plan to attend full-time.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or consider programs that allow you to demonstrate stronger performance. Raising your class standing and GPA in any future coursework would directly address the factors that most influenced this decision.
